name: Doherty Threshold
description: People stay more engaged and productive when an interactive system responds quickly enough that waiting does not break their train of thought. In design practice, this is usually summarized as keeping response times under roughly 400 ms.
design_relevance_note: Used in latency budgeting, perceived-performance work, loading states, and system-feedback design to keep interactions feeling immediate rather than stop-start.
myth_risk_note: Real partial backing already exists in the corpus for the subsecond-response-time claim generally; the specific '400 millisecond' cutoff popularized in design practice is more precise than what the existing evidence independently verifies, which is why this stays at low rather than none.
prevalence_note: Dedicated Laws of UX entry and a staple of UX performance/perceived-speed discussions, though less universal in basic design education than Fitts’s or Hick’s Law.

findings.description: In a controlled study inside a real program-development organization, programmer productivity increased by 62% when system response time was subsecond rather than slower — strong evidence that faster interactive response materially affects sustained task performance, even if it does not by itself prove a universal 400 ms cutoff for all interface contexts.
findings.effect_size: 62% productivity increase with subsecond response time
findings.source_title: A comparative study of system response time on program developer productivity

applications.title: Amazon's latency A/B tests -- and the '100ms = 1% of sales' statistic, which traces to a single slide with no published data
applications.description: Greg Linden, a former Amazon software engineer, wrote on his own blog (November 2006) and presented at a 2006 Stanford talk that Amazon ran real A/B tests deliberately delaying page loads in 100-millisecond increments, finding that 'even very small delays would result in substantial and costly drops in revenue.' His blog wording is qualitative. His Stanford slides carry the now-ubiquitous figure as a single bullet ('+100 ms -1% sales @ Amazon'), and that slide is the origin of the statistic repeated across web-performance writing -- that every 100ms of latency costs 1% of sales. No methodology, sample or underlying data has been published for the figure, so it can be cited as Linden's reported result but not as an independently verified measurement. The underlying phenomenon -- that response times need to stay under a threshold before delay measurably breaks engagement, the Doherty Threshold's own subject matter -- is real and consistent with Linden's account.
applications.industry_context: E-commerce; this account and its widely repeated one-slide statistic are now foundational reference points across web-performance engineering generally.
applications.ethical_note: A technical performance-optimization finding with no persuasion or manipulation dimension -- included here for its citation-accuracy value (the widely repeated figure traces to a single slide without published data) rather than for any ethical concern in the underlying practice itself.
